2.0.0.en: 1 For in the error of their thoughts they said within themselves: "Our life is short and wretched, and there is no remedy for the death of man, and it was never known that any man returned from Hades.

2.0.1.en: For they (the wicked) thought wrongly, and said to one another:

2.0.2.en: "Our life is short and tedious, and there is no remedy for the end of man, and it was never known that any man returned from the grave. [1]

2.0.3.en: It is clear that the writer is Solomon the Wise, for until his time they had not heard of a dead person rising, whereas in the days of Elijah and also Elisha, the first raised the son of the widow after his crying to the Lord (1 Kgs 17:20-22), and the dead man who touched the bones of the prophet Elisha rose (2 Kgs 13:21).

2.0.4.en: Someone may say: Was this not the view of righteous Job, who cursed the day in which he was born (Job 3)?

2.0.5.en: Far apart is Job's speech about the shortness of life from the speech of the wicked, for although Job was greatly embittered by the weight of trials and the accusations of his friends and their enmity toward him, and he longed for death, yet he often hoped for the just divine judgment and for the resurrection from the dead. But the wicked in their gloomy view of life denied the resurrection.

2.0.6.en: The shortness of life is something no one can deny, but the righteous looks at his life as a bridge to cross over to eternity with joy and gladness, while the wicked is crushed by the darkness in his heart, so despair dominates him, and instead of preparing for eternal life by enjoying the righteousness of Christ, he walks in a spirit of selfishness.

2.0.7.en: The divine Word became incarnate, and walked the way of our temporal life, and accepted death in the prime of His youth, that by His resurrection we may hope for the resurrection, and according to the shortness of our life on the earth as a joyful divine gift.

2.0.8.en: St. Augustine sees that the Lord Christ appeared to the Apostles after His resurrection for no purpose but to confirm the resurrection of the body. [He wished to teach us nothing but that we must believe in the resurrection of the dead.]

2.0.9.en: * Truly our faith in the resurrection of our Lord from the dead and His ascension into the heavens supports our faith with a great hope. For this doctrine shows us strongly how He of His own will, He who has the power to lift up His life, laid it down for our sake. How great is the confidence which the hope of the believers inspires when they realize the greatness of the things He endured for the sake of men who were not yet believers! When it was expected that He would come from heaven as Judge of the living and the dead, the negligent were in great terror, but when they consecrated their lives with great striving they were filled with longing for Him, walking in a holy life instead of fearing His coming because of the evil of their life.

2.0.10.en: * It is a sure hope... it has already become present and we have acquired it in practice; our future life has now been accomplished in our Head and Mediator who rose from the dead, the man Jesus Christ.

2.0.11.en: St. Augustine * If you believe that Christ has risen from the dead, you must believe that you also have risen with Him in like manner. And if you believe that He sits at the right hand of the Father in the heavens, you must believe that you are no longer henceforth in the earthly scene, but in the heavenly. And if you believe that you have died with Christ, you must believe that you shall live with Him. And if you believe that Christ is dead to sin and alive to God, you also must be dead to sin and alive to God.

2.0.12.en: This is because the man who (sets his mind on things above) shows his faith in Him who raised Jesus from the dead. And as for this man, "his faith is counted for righteousness". For if we have risen with Christ, who is the Righteousness, and walk in newness of life, and live according to righteousness, then Christ has risen for us, that we may be justified.. since we have taken on a new life after the likeness of His resurrection."

2.0.13.en: Origen * Thinking that is not simple causes a man to lose his hope in the last coming of the Lord (the Parousia), which drives him to evil conduct.

2.0.14.en: St. Clement of Rome * He appeared to put an end to the sins of the Jews, and that we may be saved through the Heir, the Lord Jesus, who was prepared to come into the world, and by His coming save our souls that walk in the ravines of death and are given over to the evil way.

2.1.s.en: 2. A life at the mercy of the winds

2.1.0.en: 2 For we are born at all adventure: and we shall be hereafter as though we had never been: for the breath in our nostrils is as smoke, and speech a spark from the movement of our heart: 3 which being extinguished, our body shall be turned into ashes, and our spirit shall vanish as the soft air, and our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist, that is driven away with the beams of the sun, and overcome with the heat thereof. 4 And after a while our name shall be forgotten, and no man shall have our works in remembrance.

2.1.1.en: We were born by chance, and hereafter we shall be as though we had never been, for the breath in our nostrils is smoke, and speech is a spark from the beating of our hearts. [2]

2.1.2.en: The wicked in their conduct embrace a practical atheism, looking at man's life as the offspring of sheer chance, with no place in their minds for God's plan, and looking at bodily death as the end of life, with no other life and no resurrection.

2.1.3.en: The wicked view life as the enjoyment of pleasures and temporal merriment, for unbelief destroys all hope in men, so they feel their existence as though it were nonexistence; their spirits are not from God but are smoke that quickly vanishes never to return, and their bodies turn into ashes scattered as by the winds.

2.1.4.en: One of the most important points in Origen's eschatological thought is his understanding of the Christian hope in the resurrection. In the preface to his book De Principiis he mentioned among the teachings defined in the preaching of the Church the faith that the soul has its own substance and life, which continues after death, to experience reward or punishment for its conduct, and expects that a time will come for the resurrection from the dead. He also spoke afterward in the same work of the resurrection of the body, and holds that this body will rise a spiritual body, quite different in its form from what it is at present.

2.1.5.en: In the final chapter of the book he demonstrated in a positive manner the immortality of the soul, reckoning it evil that what is in man in the likeness of God, such as the human mind, could perish entirely.

2.2.0.en: When it is extinguished, the body shall be turned into ashes, and the spirit shall vanish as the empty air [3]

2.2.1.en: These are the thoughts that the wicked turn into philosophies, whose aim is to justify man's practicing evils without restraint. Many philosophers believed in the complete annihilation of the body and soul.

2.2.2.en: When man isolates himself from God he sees himself trivial, of no value, like nothingness, but in God he sees himself the object of the love of the Creator of heaven and earth, who set him as a ruler to govern the world in righteousness and holiness, and he sees himself the very dear son of his heavenly Father.

2.2.3.en: * (Christ) is the word of truth, the word of incorruption, who renews the human person by raising him to the truth. He urges us to the salvation that abolishes corruption and takes away death.

2.2.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria Origen spoke clearly that anyone who despises the resurrection of the dead as the Church believes has no hope in Christ, unless he believes that the soul lives and is refreshed and does not receive this body in the resurrection but a body of an exalted kind. However, the Fathers of the Church affirm that the risen body is the same body that struggled with the soul in this world, but it bears a glorious nature fitting for eternal life.

2.2.5.en: * It is fitting that we do not doubt that our mortal body will rise again at the end of the world... This is the Christian faith, this is the faith of the Catholic Church, this is the apostolic faith.

2.2.6.en: St. Augustine * Just as the kingdom of darkness and sin remains hidden in the soul until the day of resurrection, when the bodies of sinners are overwhelmed by the darkness now hidden in the soul, so the kingdom of light and the heavenly image, Jesus Christ, now shines secretly within the soul and reigns in the souls of the saints. He is hidden from the eyes of men, but the eyes of the soul alone behold Christ truly until the day of resurrection comes, when the body also will be flooded with the light of the Lord and glorified by it, that light which is now hidden in the soul of man.

2.2.7.en: * Just as the fire that burned on the altar in Jerusalem was buried in a pit during the period of the captivity, and when peace came and the captives returned to Jerusalem this same fire was renewed and burned as it had before the captivity (2 Macc 1:18-33), so now the heavenly fire works in this body which we are used to, this body which in its dissolution (by death) turns into stench, and renews this body and raises it after it has decayed. For the inner fire that now dwells in the heart will then be revealed from outside and accomplish the resurrection of the body.

2.3.0.en: St. Macarius the Great And our name shall be forgotten in time, and no man shall have our works in remembrance, and our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist, that is driven away with the beams of the sun, and overcome with the heat thereof. [4]

2.3.1.en: The wicked unbelievers see their life as a mist driven away by the ray of the sun, then condensed by the heat of the sun, turning into water that falls on the earth, and the earth drinks it and it has no more existence. With the passing of the life, which the wicked liken to a cloud that passes so that the sun appears, they believe that not even a remembrance remains for man among the coming generations. The wicked man sees no difference between the portion of the wicked and the righteous after death.

2.3.2.en: Holy Scripture affirms: "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot" (Prov 10:7). And the Lord gives a promise to the righteous: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off" (Isa 56:5). Such a promise has no place in the thought or in the heart of the wicked.

2.4.0.en: 5 For our life is a shadow that passeth away; and after our end there is no returning: for it is sealed up, so that no man cometh again. 6 Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us speedily use the creatures while we are in youth, 7 let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, and let no flower of the spring pass by us: 8 let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they be withered, and let there be no meadow through which our pleasure doth not pass. 9 Let none of us go without his part of our voluptuousness: let us leave tokens of our joyfulness in every place: for this is our portion, and our lot is this.

2.4.1.en: For our days are the passing of a very shadow, and our end has no returning, because it is sealed, so that no man cometh again. [5]

2.4.2.en: The wicked see that their life passes like a shadow, and here they do not mean merely the shortness of temporal life, but its total vanishing into nothing, formed like a shadow out of nothing and ending in nothing, which drives them to immerse themselves in pleasures. But the Apostle James, when he says: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away" (Jas 4:4), by its vanishing in this world we enjoy a new, eternal life, so he adds: "Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin" (Jas 4:17). The wicked's sense of the shortness of life corrupts them, and the righteous's sense of it drives them to greater striving.

2.4.3.en: In great despair the wicked believe in the shortness of life, where there is no escape from death and no return from the grave. But the righteous, as they believe in the surpassing providence of God and His plan, realize that "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Eccl 3:1), so life is not the offspring of chance, and events do not come to pass without divine management. The wise man realizes that his creation is a divine gift, and that his life has a glorious mission that fulfills God's plan toward him.

2.5.0.en: Come on therefore, let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us make use of creation with the ardor of youth. [6]

2.5.1.en: The wicked focus on present good things, or temporal pleasures, instead of eternal glories. As though their short life were an opportunity to make use of creation by every means in the ardor of youth, that is, like those who have strength and power, enjoying good things before old age and weakness come.

2.6.0.en: Let us be drunk with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of spring pass by us. [7]

2.6.1.en: Although they realize that temporal things are temporary and passing, yet because they feel that they are on their way to nothingness and that there is no immortality for man, there is no room for striving for the holy life in the Lord, but luxury and pleasure are their enjoyment before corruption comes, whether to matter or to themselves. Their joy is poured out in pleasure. But the believer perceives the love of God the Creator in the beautiful world He brought into being for him, yet finds his enjoyment in offering thanks to the Creator for His gifts, and not in enslavement to matter. He cherishes the exercise of the freedom that was granted him, so he remains always master of matter and not its slave.

2.6.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria says that food is not a goal that we desire, but a means of life, so the Word of God, not the desire for food, leads us to the enjoyment of eternity.

2.6.3.en: * Food is not to be our chief concern, nor our enjoyment and aim in life, but a means for our life, which the Lord, the "Word", arranges to lead us to eternity...

2.6.4.en: They did not realize that God gave His creature man food and drink that he may live and continue in life, and not for pleasure...

2.6.5.en: We were created not to eat and drink but to consecrate ourselves to the knowledge of God.. for the belly of the wicked is never satisfied (Prov 13:5), for it is filled with an appetite that is not satisfied and not quenched.

2.6.6.en: * We must have a kind of discernment with regard to food, so that food is simple, very ordinary, suitable for simple children.. it prepares for a life that stands on two essentials, health and strength. This accords with food being simple and uncomplicated, so that it is easy to digest, makes the body light and agile, and brings growth and health.

2.6.7.en: The wretched art of cookery spoils the taste, as happens in the art of making sweets and pastries.

2.6.8.en: The human body gains no benefit from extravagance in kinds of food; on the contrary, those who use the minimum of food are stronger and healthier and more honorable and dignified, so we see servants healthier than their masters, and peasants sounder in body than the owners of estates.

2.6.9.en: * The philosophers are wiser than the rich, for they do not bury the mind under heaps of food, nor deceive themselves with pleasures and enjoyments, but the feast of love "agape" `agapy is in the heavenly food, and in the feast of the mind and sound thinking...

2.6.10.en: The glutton is like one who buries his mind in his belly.

2.6.11.en: St. Clement of Alexandria As for drunkenness with wine and putting wreaths of flowers on the heads, they were among the pagan rites, connected with the practice of abominations and the worship of idols.

2.7.0.en: And let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they be withered. [8]

2.7.1.en: Theaters and arenas were usually used for celebrations of the pagan gods or of the ruler or emperor as a god, and they had their own rites, such as lighting torches and putting wreaths of flowers on their heads. Some Christians in the first centuries, because of the simple or the weak in faith, were compelled to refuse the use of flowers, not because they are unclean, but because they were associated with the worship of Satan and idols. Yet the martyr Justin (110-165) says:

2.7.2.en: [Everything that is born as the inviolable gift of God cannot be violated by a human act (even if it is used in pagan rites). In any case, we abstain from using them lest anyone think that we submit to the demons for whose sake wine is drunk, or that we are ashamed of our religion.

2.7.3.en: Certainly the flowers of spring are delightful to us, for we choose the spring rose and the lily and other flowers of very joyful colors and fragrant scent, and we use them, whether each one by itself, or we scatter their petals, or weave them together as wreaths with which we adorn our necks.]

2.7.4.en: And Minucius Felix (second or third century) says that flowers are useful for the sense of smell, for the nose receives a sweet fragrance.

2.7.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria says: [Those who have been taught by the Logos refrain from wearing wreaths (of flowers). For they consider that it is not necessary to bind their minds which are in their heads, not because the wreath is a symbol of the life of unrestrained drunkenness, but because it is associated with paganism.]

2.7.6.en: Let none of us be without a share in our revelry.

2.8.0.en: Let us leave in every place tokens of our rejoicing, for this is our portion, and this is our lot. [9]

2.8.1.en: For nothing occupies them but a life of revelry or noisy carousing (revelry) and wantonness (wanton). They invite their relatives and friends to share in these dissolute parties, looking at it as life itself and gladness, and that this is the portion of the joyful man. Without it life is counted as death, without taste.

2.9.s.en: 4. Their law is the law of the jungle

2.9.0.en: 10 Let us oppress the poor righteous man, let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the ancient gray hairs of the aged of many days. 11 Let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth.

2.9.1.en: Let us oppress the poor righteous man, and let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the gray hairs of the aged of many days. [10]

2.9.2.en: The wicked in their dissolution want to silence the voice of wisdom and justice; they oppose the wise and do not care for the experience of prudent elders.

2.9.3.en: The wicked's loss of hope in immortality does not drive them to pleasure only, but they find their enjoyment in plundering others, even the poor and the widows and the aged. They have lost the feeling of love and tenderness, so their law became injustice and robbery, caring nothing for the needs of the poor, or the bitterness of soul of the widow, or the weakness of the aged. They saw that it was their right to exercise power, and that in this conduct there is justice.

2.9.4.en: By withdrawing from God, the source of love and tenderness and the practical model of sound values and principles, they lost every feeling and emotion, and their inner balances were upset; they became more hideous than beasts of prey moved by instinct and lust, which are cruel with violence without knowing it.

2.10.0.en: But let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth. [11]

2.10.1.en: The law of the wicked and their principle is not the law of God but the law of force, as being above truth. Their law is the law of the jungle. They see in love, long-suffering and endurance weakness and servility unbecoming to them.

2.10.2.en: * O you who are exalted and proud and arrogant, remember death, which will destroy your loftiness and dissolve your members and loosen the joints and bring corruption on the body in all its forms. By death the exalted are brought low, and the violent and cruel are buried in its darkness...

2.10.3.en: O you greedy plunderers who rob your companions, remember death, and do not multiply your sins. For in that place sinners do not repent, and he who robbed the possessions of his fellow does not even own his own money, but goes to the place where wealth is not used, and becomes nothing, his dignity passes away from him, and his sins remain to stand against him on the day of judgment.

2.11.0.en: 12 Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is grievous to us, and is contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the Law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our way of life. 13 He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the son of the Lord. 14 He was made a reprover of our thoughts. 15 He is grievous unto us even to behold: for his life is not like other men's, his ways are of another fashion. 16 We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and maketh his boast that God is his father. 17 Let us see if his words be true: and let us prove what shall happen in the end of him. 18 For if the just man be the son of God, he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.

2.11.1.en: Let us lie in wait for the righteous, for he troubles us, opposes our works, and blames us for our transgressions of the Law, and accuses us of being unfaithful to our teaching. [12]

2.11.2.en: The wicked did not stop at being absorbed in lusts and using violence and injustice even with the poor and needy, but they try to entrap the righteous and set snares and traps for them, because they refuse fellowship with them in their evils, and because they rebuke them for their wrong behavior, if not by words then by the conduct of the righteous. Thus the sight of the righteous becomes exceedingly grievous to them, because he rebukes them.

2.11.3.en: Some see that these expressions carry clear prophecies about our Lord Jesus Christ, the Righteous, who by His conduct as by His teachings rebuked the scribes and Pharisees, and they could not bear Him, but lay in wait to kill Him and be rid of Him by the Cross.

2.11.4.en: It is strange that the wicked do not bear the righteous even after his death, for his memory remains rebuking them. This happened with the Lord Christ even after His death and resurrection, for the Jewish leaders could not hear the name of Jesus, and the accusation directed against the Christians was the accusation of the Name. And the cries of the leaders against them were that they bring this Name upon them.

2.11.5.en: The divine light shining in the life of the righteous is not borne by the darkness lurking in the hearts of the wicked. The world in its darkness does not receive the light, and as the Lord Christ said in His farewell prayer about His disciples: "the world hath hated them, because they are not of the world" (Jn 17:14).

2.11.6.en: St. Ambrose sees that Joseph found his brethren in Dothan (Gen 37:17), which means "abandonment", and thus they represent the souls that forsake God and do not wish to come to Him to find rest in Him (Mt 11:28). These, when they saw Joseph coming from afar, rose up against him and wanted to kill him (Gen 37:28). They rose up while he was far from them; so also when the Lord Christ came to His own to draw near to them they rejected Him and planned His killing, saying what is stated in the Book of Wisdom: "Let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is grievous to us" (Wis 2:12).

2.11.7.en: * Let us flee from the peace of the wicked, for they plot against the righteous man. They gather together to press upon him who is righteous.

2.11.8.en: St. Ambrose * As the thoughts of the Jews were to do the Lord an injustice... they forgot that they were bringing wrath upon themselves, therefore the Lord wept over them (by the mouth of the prophet), saying: "Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?" (Ps 2:1).

2.11.9.en: Truly vain is the thinking of the Jews, for they think death against Life, and devise unreasonable things against the Word of the Father!

2.11.10.en: And he who now looks at their dispersion and the ruin of their city says: "Woe unto them, for they have devised evil against themselves"..

2.11.11.en: This is good, my brethren, for since they sinned against Holy Scripture they did not know that "He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh down a wall, a serpent shall bite him" (Eccl 10:8).

2.11.12.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic * They bound Jesus and brought Him to the house of the high priest. Do you want to know how this too was written beforehand? Isaiah says: [Woe unto their souls! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves, saying, Let us bind the righteous; because he is closed to us] (see Isa 3:9; Wis 2:12). Yes, woe unto their souls.

2.11.13.en: That you may see how this is: Isaiah was sawn asunder, and afterward the people were set right. Jeremiah was cast into a pit of mire, but the wound of the Jews was healed, for their iniquities were few because they were directed against a man. But when the Jews sinned against God made man it was said: "Woe unto their souls... Let us bind the righteous!"

2.11.14.en: Was He not able to set Himself free?! Someone may say: He who loosed Lazarus from the bands of death on the fourth day, and set Paul free from the iron fetters of prison, was He not able to set Himself free?

2.11.15.en: The angels stood ready saying: "Let us break their bands asunder" (Ps 2:3), but they held back, because their Master willed to accept this.

2.11.16.en: He was led to the court before the elders. And this is a testimony of that: "The Lord will enter into judgment with the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof" (Isa 3:14).

2.12.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the son of the Lord. [13]

2.12.1.en: Since Jesus the Righteous rebuked the Jews in many places (Mt 25; Jn 8), and revealed to them their sickness, they did not bear this world but sought to kill Him, "because he not only had broken the sabbath, but said also that God was his Father, making himself equal with God" (Jn 5:18).

2.13.0.en: He became a reproach to our thoughts. [14]

2.13.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that God does not separate the righteous from the wicked, but allows them to mingle together for the benefit of both sides. The wicked look at the righteous, and the righteousness of the righteous rebukes them, and on the other side this is counted a gain for the righteous in that they are a cause for the repentance of some of the wicked.

2.13.2.en: Even the sight of him is grievous to us.

2.14.0.en: For his life is not like the life of others, and his ways are different. [15]

2.14.1.en: He became strange in their eyes, for righteousness is to them weakness and cowardice, and violence and plunder are strength and chivalry. Good became evil in their eyes, and evil good.

2.14.2.en: * There is a benefit for the wicked in mingling with the good, for they feel confusion, and are ashamed, and are put to shame in their presence. For even if they do not abstain from evil, they do not dare to do what they do in secret. And this is no small matter, that they do not commit transgression openly. The life of others becomes an accuser of the evil of those. Hear at least what is said of the righteous man: "He became a danger to us, even his appearance" (Wis 2:14). It is no small beginning of reform through torment in the presence of (the righteous man).

2.14.4.en: The mere looking at the righteous man is hateful to sinners. "Even his appearance is grievous to us" (Wis 2:15). For they cannot bear his splendor, like diseased eyes that cannot bear the rays of the sun.

2.14.5.en: But to many it is grievous not only to see him but even to hear of him.

2.14.6.en: St. John Chrysostom We are esteemed of him as counterfeits, and he avoids our ways as he avoids uncleanness.

2.15.0.en: He pronounceth the end of the righteous to be blessed, and maketh his boast that God is his father. [16]

2.15.1.en: It is not fitting for the righteous to despise sinners, nor to condemn them, although he does not accept their evils and does not walk in their ways. It is not fitting for him to insult them even by his looks, but to be gentle with them and love them in the Lord, seeking their salvation. But the wicked, knowing the corruption of their ways and the righteous man's refusal to walk with them in the same way, realize that he is teaching them that their way is vain and false, and that he avoids their ways because he blesses the end of the righteous and cherishes the spirit of sonship to God, this spirit which the rich grace of God gave him in the waters of Baptism.

2.15.2.en: But what is the reaction of the wicked who persist in their evil? They say:

2.16.0.en: Let us see whether his words are true, and let us prove what shall happen in the end of him. [17]

2.16.1.en: Instead of imitating the righteous, they mock them, as they mocked the Holy Righteous One, the only-begotten Son of God.

2.17.s.en: 6. Opposition to the righteous even unto death

2.17.0.en: 19 Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his patience. 20 Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for he shall be visited, as he saith.

2.17.1.en: For if the righteous man be the son of God, he will help him, and deliver him from the hand of his enemies. [18]

2.17.2.en: The wicked cherish their brute strength and think that there is no power able to stand before them, not even God Himself. And as they wrong the righteous they mock him, saying: "If the righteous be the son of God, let him help him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies". Thus they challenge God Himself, whether He is able to deliver the righteous from their hands.

2.17.3.en: Here is a clear prophecy about the Lord Christ, when they mocked Him, so that the two thieves said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save". And it was said of Him: "If he be the Son of God, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him". They did not realize that by the Cross the Lord Christ triumphed over Satan, and by His death trampled death, and saved all mankind that it might triumph and be crowned by Him.

2.17.4.en: Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness and prove his patience. [19]

2.17.5.en: This challenge was present between Satan, personally or through his party which entered into covenant with him, and God in the persons of His believers among the men of the Old and New Testaments, and it reached its peak at the coming of His only-begotten Son, for the enemy of good thought that he was able to be rid of Him completely by the Cross, as the enemy was ignorant of His humility and His plan for the salvation of the world. And this challenge remains between the world which lies in the wicked one and the Church of God, increasing until it reaches its peak with the coming of the Antichrist in the last days, when the enemy of good realizes that his end has come very near.

2.18.0.en: Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for he shall be visited, according to his words". [20]

2.18.1.en: Both St. Augustine and Origen see that the wicked condemn the Righteous One, our Lord Jesus, to a shameful death, that is, the Cross, and did not realize that by the Cross He was at the peak of glory through His love and humility.

2.18.2.en: * Behold, we see this prophecy (Wis 2:12-21) in the form of a longing and a prayer fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

2.18.3.en: St. Augustine * He was glorified when He came to the Cross and when He endured death. Do you want to know that He was glorified? He Himself said: "Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son also may glorify thee" (Jn 17:1). Bearing the Cross was glory to Him, but His glory was not in a beautiful appearance but in humility. For it was said of Him: [He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross] (see Phil 2:8). And the prophet prophesied of this, saying: "Let us condemn him with a shameful death" (Wis 2:20). And Isaiah says of Him: "From oppression and from judgment he was taken" (Isa 53:8).

2.18.4.en: Origen And as the enemy wished to be rid of the Lord Christ by the Cross, so he does not cease to strive to kill the believers and destroy them from their birth. Origen comments on the statement: "And Pharaoh charged all his people, saying, Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive" (Ex 2:22), saying:

2.18.5.en: [Do you see what the ruler of this world commands his servants? He commands to steal our children and cast them into the river, and to set snares continually from their birth. He commands to attack them from the moment they begin to touch the breasts of the Church and asks to tear them away from her and pursue them until the waves of the world swallow them...

2.18.6.en: Consider the danger that threatens you from your birth, or rather from your new birth, that is, immediately from your receiving Baptism... For Jesus was led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted of the devil (Mt 4:1).

2.18.7.en: This is Pharaoh's command to his people concerning the children of the Hebrews, that is, to attack them and prey on them at the moment of their birth and drown them... But Christ conquered that He might open to you the way of victory; He conquered while fasting that you also may realize how to cast out this kind by fasting and prayer (Mk 9:29).]

2.19.0.en: 21 Such things they did imagine, and were deceived: for their own wickedness hath blinded them. 22 As for the mysteries of God, they knew them not: neither hoped they for the wages of righteousness, nor discerned a reward for blameless souls. 23 For God created man to be immortal, and made him to be an image of his own eternity. 24 Nevertheless through envy of the devil came death into the world: 25 and they that do hold of his side do find it.

2.19.1.en: Thus they reasoned, but they were deceived, for their wickedness blinded them. [21]

2.19.2.en: Their pride prevents them from reviewing themselves, so they remained fixed in ignorance, error and spiritual blindness.

2.19.3.en: Their immersion in evil blinded them from seeing the wisdom of God in His long-suffering, giving them an opportunity for repentance, and how He proves the righteous by their enduring sufferings that they may receive crowns of glory in heaven. They did not realize the power working in the life of the children of God, which gives them peace in the midst of tribulations and a sense of God's presence with them, so that they rejoice and exult in the midst of sufferings.

2.19.4.en: * These flourish in the happiness of this world, and perish by the power of God. It is not that while they flourish they perish by the same thing; for they flourish for a time and perish eternally. They flourish in unreal good things, and perish in real torments.

2.20.0.en: St. Augustine For they knew not the mysteries of God, neither hoped for the wages of righteousness, nor estimated the honor of the souls that are blameless. [22]

2.20.1.en: The wicked do not know the mysteries of God, that is, His wisdom and purposes toward man, since they do not experience them in their lives. Neither do they care about what is stated in the Law about the recompense of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked. They did not know, or ignored, what is stated in the Book of Genesis about man, that he is the image of God, and was created in His likeness (Gen 1:27). Since they do not taste the earnest of heaven here, they have no portion with the righteous in the eternal glory, and do not even believe in it.

2.20.2.en: * Those who consent to iniquity have no portion among the immortal.

2.21.0.en: St. Anthony the Great For God created man for immortality, and made him the image of His own eternity. [23]

2.21.1.en: * God was not content to create us out of nothing, but He also granted us by the grace of the Word the possibility of living according to God, but men turned their faces away from eternal things, and by the counsel of Satan turned to the works of natural corruption, and became themselves the cause of the corruption of death that befell them. For they were, as I said before, corruptible, but by the grace of their participation in the Word they could have escaped natural corruption had they remained good. And because the Word dwelt in them, their natural corruption did not touch them, as the Book of Wisdom says: "God created man for immortality, and made him in the image of His eternity, but through the envy of the devil death entered into the world".

2.21.2.en: And after this happened men began to die. This is with regard to time, for corruption began to reign over them...

2.22.0.en: Pope Athanasius the Apostolic But through the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and they that are of his party experience it. [24]

2.22.1.en: "Death" here is the spiritual death under which the wicked fall.

2.22.2.en: Man has no real enemy but the devil, who does not despair of working constantly to bring the greatest possible number of mankind to himself, for no purpose but to share with him the destruction that comes upon him. The devil uses every means, sometimes hidden and sometimes open, such as making man doubt God, and drawing him by pleasures.

2.22.3.en: * What does he mean by saying: "Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world"? You see that this evil beast saw that the first man was created immortal, so by his evil venom he led him to disobey the commandment, and by it he brought death upon himself. So envy caused deception, and deception disobedience, and disobedience death.

2.22.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * Envy always follows the way of virtue. As Horace says, even the top of the mountain is struck by lightning. It is not surprising to declare this to men and women, when we see that the envy of the Pharisees succeeded in crucifying our Lord Himself. All the saints have those who harbor evil wishes toward them; even Paradise (the garden) was not without the serpent through whose malice death came into the world (see 2:24).

2.22.5.en: St. Jerome * In fact there is a conflict between virtue and the envy of (the devil). The one strains every nerve to overcome goodness, and the other endures everything that man may live unsubdued. The one works to make the way of vice easy, and the other holds fast to goodness even if man suffers more troubles than others.

2.22.6.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus * "Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world" (Wis 2:24). Satan offered us death, but there is no compulsion on man to accept it, for Satan has nothing to bring upon you. Your consent, O man, led you to death.

2.22.7.en: * Now since death came to men from the devil, not because they are his offspring but because they imitated him, therefore he added immediately: "and they that were of his party imitated him" (see 2:24).

2.22.8.en: St. Augustine * If you examine the matter well, you will find that no harm can come to me from any man, however harmful, unless I fight against myself... If harm does reach me, the fault is not because of the attack of others but because of my lack of endurance. It is like very rich food, beneficial to the man who enjoys good health, yet harmful to the sick; it does not harm the man who takes it unless he is already sick. However that may be, you should know that the sin of envy is harder to heal than the rest of the sins, for it is the plague which the prophet symbolized by serpents: "For, behold, I will send serpents, vipers, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the Lord" (Jer 8:17).

2.22.9.en: Rightly did the prophet compare the bites of envy to the deadly venom of vipers... for they are a source of poison, but they perish and die after biting the person. So the envious does not harm the envied, but destroys himself before he harms the envied; he destroys himself before he pours the venom of death on another, because "through envy of the devil death entered into the world, and they that are of his party experience it" (Wis 2:24-25). Just as the first who perished (the devil) by envy finds no remedy for atonement nor healing, so those who allow themselves to be envious are excluded from the help of any holy charmer, for they were not tormented by the sins of others but were tormented by the superiority and success of those whom they envy. And they are ashamed to show the truth, so they look for trivial external causes by which to justify the sin, and as they constantly falsify the truth, their hope of healing remains vain, while the deadly poison runs in their veins, which they do not excrete, but which arises in them because of the success of others.

2.22.10.en: Envy is hard to heal, for in searching for its causes it becomes worse. It searches for external causes and not the inner truth, and it grows more intense when services and gifts are offered to the envious, for as Solomon himself says: "he stands before the envious" (Prov 27:4). The more the other (the envied) succeeds in submission and humility or in the virtue of patience or generosity, the more the pricks of the other's envy increase, for he desires nothing but the destruction and death of the envied.

2.22.12.en: My life is in Your hands!

2.22.13.en: * All the world knows that man's life is short, but as I am united with You my life extends into immortality.

2.22.14.en: My life is full of thorns, but it is not tedious, for I see You as my companion in the midst of sufferings.

2.22.15.en: The thorns that crowned Your head give sweetness to my sufferings!

2.22.16.en: Your death for me put to death the death that had shattered me!

2.22.17.en: Your resurrection gave me the risen life.

2.22.18.en: * I used to think that I came into the world by chance, but I realized that You were occupied with me even before my creation.

2.22.19.en: My name is engraved on Your palms, You are occupied with me and continue to work for me, that where You are I may be with You!

2.22.20.en: My life is not for amusement and jesting, but I have a heavenly aim, which divine providence has set for me.

2.22.21.en: * My soul is very precious in Your eyes, even my body, as it returns to dust, You restore it to bear heavenly glories!

2.22.22.en: You bore me wholly from corruption to incorruption.

2.22.23.en: You transferred me from the circle of death to immortality!

2.22.24.en: * I do not live here to enjoy the pleasure of eating and drinking, for You are my food and my drink, and the summit of my happiness.

2.22.25.en: I wait expectantly for when I shall enjoy You, O heavenly Manna!

2.22.26.en: * The wicked mocked You, because You are holy.

2.22.27.en: Your life became a burden to them, because it condemns them.

2.22.28.en: They were determined to be rid of You, they plotted Your killing and killed themselves.
